sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Harvesting energy from environmental sources has been of particular interest these last few years. Microgenerators that can power electronic systems are a solution for the conception of autonomous, wireless devices. They allow the removal of bulky and costly wiring, as well as complex maintenance and environmental issues for battery-powered systems. In particular, using piezoelectric generators for converting vibrational energy to electrical energy is an intensively investigated field. In this domain, it has been shown that the harvested energy can be greatly improved by the use of an original non-linear treatment of the piezoelectric voltage called SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor), which consists in intermittently switching the piezoelectric element on a resonant electrical network for a very short time. However, the integration of miniaturized microgenerators with low voltage output (e.g. MEMS microgenerators) has not been widely studied. In the case of low voltage output, the losses introduced by voltage gaps of discrete components such as diodes or transistors can no longer be neglected. Therefore the purpose of this paper is to propose a model that takes into account such losses as well as a new architecture for the SSHI energy harvesting circuit that limits such losses in the harvesting process. While most of the study uses an externally powered microcontroller for the non-linear treatment, this circuit is fully self-powered, thus providing an enhanced autonomous microgenerator. In particular this circuit aims at limiting the effect of non-linear components with a voltage gap such as diodes. It is shown both theoretically and experimentally that the harvested power can be significantly increased using such a circuit. In particular, experimental measurements performed on a cantilever beam show that the circuit allows a $160 \%$ increase of the harvested power compared to a standard energy harvesting circuit, while the classical implementation of the SSHI shows an increase of only $100 \%$ of the output power in the classical case.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Thanks to the progress in microelectronics and in energy harvesting, the conception of truly autonomous devices is no longer chimerical [1]. Combined with the increasing demand in fully autonomous networks, the domain of sensing is about to experience a technological rupture with the conception of fully self-powered, wireless devices with local processing and communication abilities. Such systems, having the possibility of scavenging the energy from environmental sources such as heat, magnetic field or photons, would supply microelectronic circuits to complete different functions [2–7].

In particular, using the piezoelectric effect for converting mechanical energy into electrical energy has been extensively studied these last few years [8–15]. It has therefore been shown that applying a non-linear treatment to the piezoelectric voltage can greatly enhance the electromechanical conversion and thus the amount of energy harvested. In this domain, the parallel SSHI technique introduced by Guyomar, Richard et al, etc, has been proven to be an efficient way for harvesting energy from vibrations in a fully self-powered manner [16–19]. A similar technique, called series SSHI, has also been proposed by Taylor et al in [20].

![](images/545931715cd10c4229d8cd0df747a7fe963be8dc73eff26da11ecde0247b36eb.jpg)  
Figure 1. Standard circuit.

However, the need of integration limits the voltage output of the piezoelectric elements. Consequently voltage gaps introduced by non-linear elements such as diode bridge rectifiers need to be as small as possible. In particular, using the self-powered SSHI technique induces supplementary voltage gaps that need to be addressed. Makihara et al in [21] proposed a structure that reduces these losses, leading to a gain of approximately $20 \%$ compared to the classical implementation of the parallel SSHI. However, in this case the command of the non-linear treatment is quite complex and requires an externally powered DSP (Makihara used a DSpace interface connected with a PC, for example), making the technique useless for truly autonomous devices, as the amount of harvested energy is often below a few tens of milliwatts (while the DSP requires much more).

Thus the purpose of this paper is twofold. First, it aims at identifying the impact of voltage gaps that induce losses in the harvested energy. Also, the impact of these gaps in terms of harvested energy is derived analytically. Second, this paper proposes a new architecture for the series SSHI that can be truly self-powered, thus addressing the issue of harvesting environmental energy for truly autonomous devices. Theoretical predictions are confirmed by experimental measurement that shows that the harvested energy gain is more than $160 \%$ compared to the harvested energy using a standard circuit (while the classical implementation of the series SSHI leads to an gain of $100 \%$ ). This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 exposes the principles of the energy harvesting circuit. Section 3 proposes a theoretical development of the harvested energy for the different techniques and considering voltage gaps of the harvesting circuits. Section 4 addresses the issue of self-powering these circuits. Theoretical predictions are then compared to experimental measurements in section 5. Finally, section 6 concludes the paper.

sections.heading: 2. Principles
sections.text: This section aims at exposing the principles of energy harvesting using either the standard technique, where the piezoelement is directly connected to a diode bridge rectifier, or the series SSHI technique, that includes electronic switches connected in series with the piezoelement.

sections.heading: 2.1. Standard technique
sections.text:
The circuit of the standard energy harvesting technique is presented in figure 1. The piezoelement, which has a blocking capacitance $C _ { 0 }$ , is directly connected to a diode bridge rectifier $\mathrm { D } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { D } _ { 2 } , \mathrm { D } _ { 3 } , \mathrm { D } _ { 4 } )$ and the energy is harvested on a storage capacitor $C _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ that is connected to the load $R _ { \mathrm { L } }$ . When the absolute value of the piezoelement voltage is less than the storage capacitor voltage $V _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ plus the diode bridge rectifier voltage, then the piezoelement is in open-circuit condition and the piezoelectric voltage varies with the displacement. When the absolute value of the piezoelement voltage is equal to the storage capacitor voltage plus the diode bridge rectifier voltage, then there is an energy transfer from the piezoelectric element to the storage capacitor through $\mathrm { D } _ { 1 }$ (resp. $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ ) and $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ (resp. $\mathrm { D } _ { 4 }$ ) when the piezoelectric voltage is positive (resp. negative). Figure 2 depicts the typical waveforms of the standard energy harvesting technique.

![](images/e262b942ec943b3665cc379a86d48262083e3ee807e6cb55778f43da50eddb06.jpg)  
Figure 2. Standard technique waveforms.

sections.heading: 2.2. SSHI
sections.text:
Classical and new circuits for piezoelectric energy harvesting using the so-called SSHI are presented in figure 3. $\mathrm { S } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathbf { S } _ { 2 }$ are electronic switches that are closed when the piezoelectric voltage reaches a maximum and a minimum, respectively. These switches are closed for a very brief time period compared to the piezoelectric voltage period, thus shaping an oscillating network with the inductor $L$ . The new circuit consists in separating the maximum and minimum detection switches and replacing the diodes $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ by these switches. Such a circuit presents two advantages. First, the circuit includes less components, thus reducing the cost and the dimensions of the circuit. However, its main benefit is the removal of diodes that induce voltage gaps. Therefore losses introduced by such voltage gaps in the harvesting circuit are limited and the harvested power is thus greater. In the case of the classical SSHI circuit, there is a current flow through $L , S _ { 1 }$ (resp. $\mathbf { S } _ { 2 }$ ), $\mathrm { D } _ { 1 }$ (resp. $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ ), $C _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ and $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ (resp. $\mathrm { D } _ { 4 }$ ) when the piezovoltage reaches a maximum (resp. minimum) that charges the storage capacitor $C _ { S }$ . The same process occurs for the new proposed technique, but $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ are replaced by $\mathrm { S } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathbf { S } _ { 2 }$ , respectively. Thus the energy transfer is done through $\mathrm { D } _ { 1 }$ (resp. $\mathbf { S } _ { 2 }$ ), $C _ { S }$ and $\mathrm { S } _ { 1 }$ (resp. $\mathrm { D } _ { 4 }$ ) when the piezovoltage reaches a maximum (resp. minimum). Consequently this circuit eliminates the diodes $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ , thus removing the voltage gaps introduced by these diodes. For the two circuits, the piezoelectric element is left in open-circuit $S _ { 1 }$ and $\mathbf { S } _ { 2 }$ open) the rest of the time.

![](images/227fd7fbe319ce2e5cebc8b84fcce211b91004e182adcb31f72757ba0b7a440a.jpg)  
Figure 3. SSHI circuits: (a) classical circuit (refer to [20]); (b) new circuit for low voltage output.

![](images/9e9af9c4cc72730b58942016b418615e80b064b072c5ae5aed5039983ed9fb7b.jpg)  
Figure 4. SSHI waveforms.

The closing time period $t _ { i }$ (1) of the switches is given as half the pseudo-period of the $L C _ { 0 }$ network (as $V _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ is considered constant3, the storage capacitor has no effect), therefore leading to an inversion of the piezoelectric voltage as depicted in figure 4. However, this inversion is not perfect due to the internal losses of the circuit, and is characterized by the coefficient $\gamma$ that is related to the electrical quality factor $Q _ { i }$ as (2). Moreover in the series SSHI the inversion is done relative to the voltage $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ (resp. $- V _ { \mathrm { S } } )$ when the voltage is maximum (resp. minimum), with $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ equal to the storage capacitor voltage plus the voltage gap introduced by the switches and the diodes. As well, the extremum detection introduces a delay $\phi$ between the actual occurrence of an extremum and the switch time instant. This delay is related to the necessary voltage gap between the piezovoltage and the envelope detector voltage (as explained in section 4) for detecting an extremum. Therefore for high voltage values this delay is negligible, which is, however, not the case for systems with low voltage output:

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { t _ { i } = \pi \sqrt { L C _ { 0 } } } } \\ { { \gamma = \mathrm { e } ^ { - \pi / ( 2 Q _ { i } ) } . } } \end{array}
$$

sections.heading: 3. Theoretical development
sections.text:
From the principles presented in the previous section it is possible to derive the theoretical expression of the expected output power of the piezoelectric microgenerator. This is the purpose of the present section, which aims at giving the theoretical expressions of the output power using either the standard technique or the series SSHI (both for the classical and the new circuits). As previously shown, this paper focuses on microgenerators with low voltage input, and therefore the voltage gaps introduced by non-linear components will be taken into account. For the derivation of the theoretical output power of the microgenerator, it is considered that the system (e.g. a cantilever beam bonded by piezoelectric inserts) is excited near one of its resonance frequencies on a single mode (e.g. first flexural mode). In this case, it has been shown [22] that the output current $I$ of the piezoelectric device is given by (3), with $\dot { u }$ and $\dot { V }$ the derivatives of the displacement and the piezovoltage, respectively, and $\alpha$ and $C _ { 0 }$ the force factor and the blocking capacitance of the piezoelectric element, respectively:

$$
I = \alpha \dot { u } - C _ { 0 } \dot { V } .
$$

sections.heading: 3.1. Standard technique
sections.text:
In the case of the standard technique, the harvesting energy process occurs when the piezovoltage is not in open-circuit condition and equals the voltage $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ . Considering figure 1, the voltage $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ is given by (4), where $V _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ is the storage capacitor voltage (assumed constant) and $V _ { \mathrm { { D } } }$ is the voltage gap across a single diode. The energy harvested during a single phase (e.g. $V$ positive) is given by (5) from (3), where $u _ { \mathbf { M } }$ and $u _ { 1 }$ are the displacement magnitude and the displacement when the piezovoltage reaches $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ , respectively. The expression of $u _ { 1 }$ is derived considering the open-circuit state of the piezoelement. In this case, $I ~ = ~ 0$ and consequently $V$ varies accordingly to the displacement as (6), with $A$ an integration constant. This constant is calculated considering the previous energy extraction process (e.g. $V$ negative). Indeed, the piezoelement is in open-circuit when the displacement reaches its minimal value $- u _ { \mathrm { M } }$ for this process. At this instant, the value of the piezovoltage is $- V _ { S }$ , and therefore $A$ is given as (7). The displacement reaches $u _ { 1 }$ when the piezovoltage reaches $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ , leading to the expression of the displacement $u _ { 1 }$ as (8). Therefore the harvested energy for a single extraction process is given as (9). As such a process occurs twice a period (once for positive voltage and once for negative voltage), the output power of the microgenerator using the standard energy harvesting technique is given by (10), with $f _ { 0 }$ the frequency of vibration. The maximal harvested power for a given vibration magnitude is given under condition (11), yielding the maximal harvested power (12):

$$
V _ { \mathrm { { S } } } = V _ { \mathrm { { D C } } } + 2 V _ { \mathrm { { D } } }
$$

$$
E _ { \mathrm { s t a n d } } = \int V _ { \mathrm { D C } } I { \mathrm { d } } t = \alpha V _ { \mathrm { D C } } ( u _ { \mathrm { M } } - u _ { 1 } )
$$

$$
V = { \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } } u + A
$$

$$
- V _ { \mathrm { S } } = - { \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } } u _ { \mathrm { M } } + A \Rightarrow A = { \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } } u _ { \mathrm { M } } - V _ { \mathrm { S } }
$$

$$
V _ { \mathrm { S } } = { \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } } u _ { 1 } + A \Rightarrow u _ { 1 } = 2 { \frac { C _ { 0 } } { \alpha } } V _ { \mathrm { S } } - u _ { \mathrm { M } }
$$

$$
E _ { \mathrm { s t a n d } } = 2 V _ { \mathrm { D C } } ( \alpha u _ { \mathrm { M } } - C _ { 0 } ( V _ { \mathrm { D C } } + 2 V _ { \mathrm { D } } ) )
$$

$$
P _ { \mathrm { s t a n d } } = 2 f _ { 0 } E _ { \mathrm { s t a n d } } = 4 f _ { 0 } V _ { \mathrm { D C } } ( \alpha u _ { \mathrm { M } } - C _ { 0 } ( V _ { \mathrm { D C } } + 2 V _ { \mathrm { D } } ) )
$$

$$
{ \frac { \partial P _ { \mathrm { s t a n d } } } { \partial V _ { \mathrm { D C } } } } = 0 \Rightarrow ( V _ { \mathrm { D C } } ) _ { \mathrm { o p t } } = { \frac { \alpha } { 2 C _ { 0 } } } u _ { \mathrm { M } } - V _ { \mathrm { D } }
$$

$$
( P _ { \mathrm { s t a n d } } ) _ { \mathrm { m a x } } = f _ { 0 } C _ { 0 } \left( \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } u _ { \mathrm { M } } - 2 V _ { \mathrm { D } } \right) ^ { 2 } .
$$

sections.heading: 3.2. Series SSHI
sections.text:
In the case of series SSHI technique proposed in [20], the energy transfer process occurs when the piezoelectric element is switched to the electrical circuit. Therefore, the energy harvested during a single switch is given as (13) from (3), with $V _ { \mathbf { M } }$ the magnitude of the piezoelectric voltage, $\phi$ the phase delay between the actual occurrence of an extremum and the corresponding switch time instant and $V _ { \mathrm { m } }$ the value of the voltage after the extraction process (figure 4). As before, $C _ { 0 }$ is the blocking capacitance of the piezoelectric element and $V _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ is the storage capacitor voltage. As the voltage inversion is done relative to the voltage $V _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ , then it is possible to express the inversion considering this voltage, as well as $V _ { \mathbf { M } }$ , $V _ { \mathrm { m } }$ , $\phi$ and the inversion factor $\gamma$ , yielding (14). As well, the piezoelectric element is left in open-circuit condition between energy extraction processes and considering the inversion time period very short compared to the vibration period leads to the expression of $V _ { \mathbf { M } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { m } }$ as a function of $\alpha$ , $C _ { 0 } , \phi$ and $u _ { \mathrm { M } }$ as (15). Thus from (14) and (15) it is possible to express the energy extracted per switch as (16)

$$
E _ { \mathrm { s s h i } } = \int V _ { \mathrm { D C } } I \mathrm { d } t = C _ { 0 } V _ { \mathrm { D C } } ( V _ { \mathrm { M } } \cos ( \phi ) + V _ { \mathrm { m } } )
$$

$$
( V _ { \mathrm { m } } + V _ { \mathrm { S } } ) = \gamma ( V _ { \mathrm { M } } \cos ( \phi ) - V _ { \mathrm { S } } )
$$

$$
V _ { \mathrm { M } } - V _ { \mathrm { m } } = ( 1 + \cos ( \phi ) ) \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } u _ { \mathrm { M } }
$$

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle E _ { \mathrm { s s h i } } = ( 1 + \cos ( \phi ) ) \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) } } \\ { { \displaystyle ~ \times ~ V _ { \mathrm { D C } } \left( \alpha \cos ( \phi ) u _ { \mathrm { M } } - C _ { 0 } V _ { \mathrm { S } } \right) . } } \end{array}
$$

In the case of the classical SSHI implementation depicted in figure 3(a), the voltage gaps are introduced by the two conducting diodes of the bridge rectifier, as well as the closed switch, giving (17), where $V _ { \mathrm { S W } }$ is the voltage gap introduced by the closed switch. Therefore the expression of the harvested power is given by (18) and the maximal harvested power is thus (19).

When using the new circuit proposed in this paper, the voltage gap is reduced to only one diode and the closed switch yielding (20), and therefore the harvested power is given by (21). Consequently in this case the maximal harvested power yields (22).

In the case of a perfect switch (i.e. $V _ { \mathrm { D } } = V _ { \mathrm { S W } } = \phi = 0 \mathrm { , }$ the expression of the harvested power thus becomes (23) and the maximal harvested power (24):

sections.heading: 3.3. Mechanical effect
sections.text:
Extracting energy from an electromechanical structure also modifies its mechanical behaviour. Such an effect can be shown using a simple electromechanically coupled spring– mass system as proposed in [22], and leading to (25), where $u$ is the flexural displacement, $F$ is the driving force and $V$ is the piezovoltage. $M$ , $C$ and $K ^ { E }$ are defined as the dynamic mass, structural damping coefficient and short-circuit stiffness, and $\alpha$ is given as the force factor:

$$
M \ddot { u } + C \dot { u } + K ^ { E } u = F - \alpha V .
$$

In the case of the standard technique, the harvesting process makes the voltage no longer in phase with the displacement, creating, from a mechanical point of view, a friction effect that leads both to an attenuation of the vibrations, and therefore to a decrease of the actual displacement, and to a drift in the resonance frequency (this latter being included within the range of short-circuit and open-circuit resonance frequencies).

Using the series SSHI generates a voltage waveform that can be divided into two functions. The first function is proportional to the displacement, as in the open-circuit state. The second one is a piecewise constant function $h$ that is generated by the non-linear processing of the SSHI. The magnitude $H$ of this function is obtained considering (26), yielding the expression of $h$ (27), with $\tau$ the switching time delay (associated with $\phi$ ):

$$
V _ { \mathrm { M } } \cos ( \phi ) + V _ { \mathrm { m } } = ( 1 + \cos ( \phi ) ) \ : H
$$

$$
h = \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \left( \frac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } u _ { \mathrm { M } } - V _ { \mathrm { S } } \right) \mathrm { s g n } \left( \dot { u } ( t - \tau ) \right) .
$$

Considering that the displacement remains purely sinusoidal, $h$ can be approximated by its first harmonic, leading to a function in phase with the displacement $h _ { u }$ and a function in phase with the velocity $h _ { v }$ defined as (28), with $\omega$ the angular frequency of vibration. Therefore, the effect of energy harvesting using the SSHI technique leads both to a change in the stiffness (and thus to a resonance frequency drift) due to the contribution of $h _ { u }$ , and to a damping effect (by a change in the structural damping coefficient) produced by $h _ { v }$ . One can note that these changes are not linear as they depend on the vibration magnitude:

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { } & { h _ { u } = \left( \cfrac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \left( \cfrac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } } - \cfrac { V _ { \mathrm { S } } } { u _ { \mathrm { M } } } \right) \sin ( \phi ) u } \\ & { } & { h _ { v } = \left( \cfrac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \left( \cfrac { \alpha } { C _ { 0 } \omega } - \cfrac { V _ { \mathrm { S } } } { u _ { \mathrm { M } } \omega } \right) \cos ( \phi ) \dot { u } . } \end{array}
$$

Considering that the structure is oscillating at its modified resonance angular frequency $\omega _ { \mathrm { r } }$ (due to the mechanical feedback) defined as (29) and that the force is in phase with the speed (i.e. low mechanical losses), then the expression of the displacement magnitude yields (30), leading to the expression of the maximal output power (31) from (16):

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \omega _ { \tau } = \sqrt { \frac { \left( K ^ { E } + \frac { \omega _ { \tau } ^ { 2 } } { c _ { 0 } } + \frac { 4 } { \pi } \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \left( \frac { \alpha } { c _ { 0 } } - \frac { V _ { \tau } } { u _ { \mathrm { s t } } } \right) \sin ( \phi ) \right) } { M } } \quad ( 2 9 ) } \\ & { u _ { \mathrm { M } } = \frac { F _ { \mathrm { M } } + \alpha _ { \tau } ^ { 4 } \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \cos ( \phi ) V _ { \mathrm { S } } } { C \omega _ { \tau } + \frac { 4 } { \pi } \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \frac { \omega _ { \tau } ^ { 2 } } { C _ { 0 } } \cos ( \phi ) } \qquad ( 3 0 ) } \\ & { \left( P _ { \mathrm { s s i n } } \right) = \frac { \omega _ { \tau } } { \pi } \left( 1 + \cos ( \phi ) \right) \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) V _ { \mathrm { D C } } } \\ & { \qquad \times \left( \alpha \cos ( \phi ) \frac { R _ { \mathrm { M } } + \alpha _ { \tau } ^ { 4 } \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \cos ( \phi ) V _ { \mathrm { S } } } { C \omega _ { \tau } + \frac { 4 } { \pi } \left( \frac { 1 + \gamma } { 1 - \gamma \cos ( \phi ) } \right) \frac { \omega _ { \tau } ^ { 2 } } { C _ { 0 } } \cos ( \phi ) } - C _ { 0 } V _ { s } \right) . } \end{array}
$$

A comparison between the two techniques taking into account the mechanical feedback is depicted in figure 5, considering the electromechanical structure presented in section 5. Although the differences in terms of output power are negligible for high force magnitude or low structural damping coefficient (corresponding to a high displacement magnitude and therefore to a high output voltage), this figure clearly shows the effectiveness of the proposed architecture over the classical implementation of the SSHI for low values of the force and high damping coefficients.

![](images/3f05967af0cbeec8da7579e237a9ba85e5e14c9c27ac8653d4612193264e6f82.jpg)  
Figure 5. Maximal harvested power as a function of the input force and structural damping coefficient (electromechanical parameters are those of the experimental structure described in section 5).

sections.heading: 4. Self-powering issues
sections.text:
Although non-linear treatments can significantly increase the efficiency of energy harvesting, the control command required to implement such treatments can be costly in terms of energy. These energy requirements are often greater than the harvested energy gain, thus seriously reducing the interest in such treatments. The enhancement proposed in this paper can be truly selfpowered by the use of the electronic breaker proposed in [23], and whose principles are given in figure 6. It consists in comparing the actual piezoelectric voltage with its envelope. When the envelope is greater than the piezovoltage, then the switch process is engaged. Such a circuit consumes very little power (roughly $5 \%$ of the total electrostatic energy available on the piezoelectric element). In the following experiments, such switches are used: one for positive switching $( \mathbf { S } _ { 1 } )$ and one for negative switching $( \mathbf { S } _ { 2 } )$ . The exact operation of this circuit is as follows. The envelope detection of the input signal is performed by ${ \mathrm { R } } _ { 3 }$ , $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ and $C$ . While this envelope is less than the input voltage, the transistor $\mathrm { T } _ { 2 }$ is blocked, and therefore $\mathrm { T _ { 1 } }$ is as well. When the difference between the input signal and the voltage of the capacitor $C$ is greater than the threshold voltage of $\mathrm { T } _ { 2 }$ , the transistor starts conducting. Therefore $\mathrm { D } _ { 3 }$ is blocked and the capacitor $C$ discharges through $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ , $\mathrm { T } _ { 2 }$ , $\mathrm { R } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathrm { T _ { 1 } }$ . Thus the two transistors conduct, initiating the switching process. The harvesting process is interrupted by $\mathrm { D } _ { 1 }$ which stops conducting when the current is null (corresponding to the end of the inversion process). At the end of the harvesting process, the charges on the capacitor $C$ are null (total discharge). $\mathrm { R } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \mathrm { R } } _ { 2 }$ ensure that the emitter–base voltages of $\mathrm { T } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathrm { T } _ { 2 }$ do not interfere with the envelope detector and capacitor $C$ , and $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 }$ ensures the proper discharge of $C$ . ![](images/674e43bf998699bb67fcf70d9cdfa6b62800ed2c3d1520334cccac2e3c947299.jpg) Figure 6. sections.heading: 5. Experimental results
sections.text: This section aims at validating the theoretical predictions presented in section 3. It is important to note that, although the structure used in this section is not a MEMS structure, it is excited with a small driving force that makes the voltage gaps of the non-linear components non-negligible. As well, these components are off-the-shelf components, and thus not optimized for energy harvesting with low voltage output.

sections.heading: 5.1. Experimental set-up
sections.text:
The experimental set-up consists of a $4 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ long cantilever steel beam clamped at one end to a rigid base and bonded by a piezoelectric insert on its surface (figure 7(a)). The beam is excited using an electromagnet, and an inductive proximity sensor is used for measuring the displacement magnitude at the free end of the beam. The electronic switch is depicted in figure 7(b), as well as the inductance used for energy harvesting using the series SSHI technique. The beam is set vibrating on its first flexural mode, corresponding to the resonance frequency $f _ { 0 }$ . Parameter identification is given in table 1. The storage capacitance value is set to $1 \ \mu \mathrm { F }$ and load resistor $R _ { \mathrm { L } }$ is made to vary in order to change the value of the voltage $V _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ and thus the harvested power. In the following it will be considered that the mechanical feedback of the energy harvesting process is negligible, the structure being weakly coupled and having relatively high internal losses.

![](images/81f9fb682f18092671e4fc710330f242712ee67db5521402eda4dddda96cd272.jpg)  
Figure 7. Experimental set-up: (a) instrumented cantilever beam; (b) unipolar electronic breaker and inductor.

sections.heading: 5.2. Experimental results and discussion
sections.text:
The first measurements consist in determining the harvested power for a constant displacement of $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ of the free end of the beam. Results are depicted in figure 8 and show good agreement with theoretical predictions. In particular, due to different voltage gaps for each technique, the optimal rectified voltage value $V _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ is different from one technique to another. Also, while the classical implementation of the series SSHI shows a gain of 2 in terms of maximal power compared to the standard energy harvesting technique, the circuit proposed in this paper allows a gain of 2.6 $30 \%$ more) in such a configuration, thus harvesting more energy by reducing voltage gaps in the harvesting circuit.

This is much truer for lower vibration magnitudes. Figure 9 shows the evolution of the maximal harvested power as a function of the free end displacement magnitude. As previously, these results show very good agreement with theoretical predictions. Performances of the new series SSHI circuit over the classical implementation are clearly shown, especially for low vibration magnitudes. In particular, whereas the classical circuit for the series SSHI does not work for a displacement magnitude less than $5 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , the new implementation allows harvesting energy as soon as the displacement magnitude reaches $3 5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . As well, the diode voltage gap removal leads to an increase of the harvested power that is roughly proportional to the displacement magnitude, and approximately equals in this case $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ for a $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ free end displacement magnitude, which is not negligible for microgenerators with low power output.

The increase of the SSHI effectiveness can also be shown considering experimental waveforms of the piezovoltage, as depicted in figure 10. The piezovoltage increase allowed by the reduction of the switching losses therefore allows a more efficient inversion and thus a greater amount of harvested energy (the available electrostatic energy on the piezoelement at the switching time instant is $50 \%$ greater with the proposed architecture).

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text:
The present paper proposes a new self-powered architecture for optimized energy harvesting using piezoelectric elements with a low voltage output, as well as a theoretical development of harvested power taking into account non-linear effects introduced by discrete components.

Taking advantage of the outstanding performance offered by the non-linear technique called series SSHI proposed by Tailor et al in [20], a new circuit is proposed for microgenerators with low voltage output. The principles of this new architecture rely on limiting voltage gaps introduced by non-linear components, such as diodes, by separating minimum and maximum detectors that are classically put together for the classical implementation of the series SSHI. This circuit is also fully self-powered, requiring no external power supply for the piezoelectric voltage treatment.

A theoretical development is proposed in order to identify significant parameters in the optimization of the circuit, and theoretical predictions are validated through experimental measurements performed on a cantilever beam. It is shown that the proposed circuit can operate below the minimum voltage of the classical series SSHI implementation, and allows a significant gain in terms of harvested power compared to standard and classical SSHI implementations. For example, under experiment conditions, the proposed circuit leads to a gain of $160 \%$ compared to the standard energy harvesting technique, while the classical implementation of the SSHI leads to an increase of only $100 \%$ .

Thus the new architecture proposed in this paper provides a new step in the integration of miniature microgenerators, such as MEMS generators.
